title: Keep Images in Sight: Visual Position Re-Anchoring for Long-Context MLLMs
abstract: Long-context multimodal intelligence requires revisiting earlier images as conversations and documents accumulate, yet retaining an image does not guarantee reliable access to its details. By varying context length, redistributing a fixed text passage around the image, and changing positions without adding text, we identify the positional relation between images and questions as a direct influence on visual access. title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference.
abstract: When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships-not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge. How such relational knowledge is represented and used in the brain remains a long-standing question in cognitive neuroscience. Here, using a behavioural task and computational modelling, we show that participants (N = 36) leveraged existing knowledge of relational structures to infer new relationships, facilitating adaptation in changing environments. Whole-brain neuroimaging identified consistent representations of relational structure in the hippocampus. To investigate the causal link between hippocampal representations and inference, we used neural network simulations to predict the behavioural effects of disrupting such representations. Consistent with this prediction, transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the human hippocampus (N = 20), transiently modulating its activity, disrupted structure-based inference (P < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.89, 95% confidence interval -1.41 to -0.36), providing empirical evidence for a causal role of hippocampus in relational-structure learning and structure-based inference.

title: Music illuminates sociocultural dimensions of autobiographical memory.
abstract: Researchers have long theorized that autobiographical memory relies on sociocultural structures, such as life scripts and event schemas. The potency of music as a marker of social and personal identity, combined with its ubiquity in everyday life, allows us to connect these everyday scripts to larger patterns of socially and culturally shaped behavior. We collected free-response descriptions of autobiographical memories evoked by short clips of familiar songs from university undergraduates (n = 233). The songs spanned three popular genres and aligned with two significant periods of listeners' lives. We analyzed the similarities and differences in the content of memories for particular songs using natural language processing. Memories cued by songs from the same category displayed striking similarities, suggesting that particular types of music cue memories that are similar between listeners but that vary according to characteristics such as music genre and release date. Two control conditions, in which a new set of participants reported memories evoked by key words from the lyrics (n = 121) and short narrative summaries of the lyrics (n = 129), indicate that these results cannot be explained by within-category similarities in the songs' lyrical content. Instead, we suggest that the intersubjective structure of music-evoked autobiographical memories reflects socioculturally-defined scripts tied to song characteristics such as genre and release date. Thus, while memories may feel idiosyncratic and personal, there are also substantial similarities in life experiences between individuals with broadly similar backgrounds, and these shared experiences can be spontaneously called to mind through the seemingly innocuous act of turning on the radio.

title: Intervening contexts reshape hippocampal-cortical retrieval states and later source attribution.
abstract: Memories are often reactivated in one context and only later judged with respect to where they originally occurred. We tested how an intervening retrieval context shapes neural representations and later source memory. In two fMRI tasks, participants (both male and female) encoded objects within contextual backgrounds, completed an immediate retrieval test in which object cues appeared against either the original background or a different background, and subsequently judged each object's original context on a neutral screen. Shifted cueing contexts reduced source accuracy and biased errors toward the intervening context, despite no detectable difference in immediate recognition or associative-memory performance. Representational similarity analyses showed that encoding patterns reflected original-context structure, whereas immediate-cue-period patterns were broadly organized by the cued (i.e., currently visible) context. On shifted trials, activity patterns showed greater similarity to encoding-derived templates for the cued context than for the original context. Across participants, greater differentiation of original-context similarity between consistent and shifted cueing in posterior hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex was associated with better source memory after a contextual shift. Within participants, precuneus contextual engagement and dorsal anterior cingulate context alignment predicted later source choices, with similar relationships after adjustment for immediate recognition responses. Later source attribution therefore depended on the contextual state expressed when an item was re-encountered, not simply on reinstatement of the original event.Significance statement Remembering is often described as bringing up the past, but memories are frequently reactivated in new contexts before we judge where they came from. We show that this intervening context can bias later source attribution even when that context is no longer visible at final test. Using two fMRI tasks, representational similarity analysis and trial-level source-choice models, we found that cue-period activity was organized by the context present during cueing and that specific context-state signals predicted later memory choices, whereas item reinstatement did not. Source-memory errors can therefore reflect contextual information encountered after the original event, not only failures to recover the original context.

title: Posterior alpha/beta oscillations reflect oculomotor dynamics underlying subsequent memory effects
abstract: Abstract Neural activity and eye movements are well-established predictors of human memory performance. Successful memory formation is associated with reduced alpha/beta power and increased eye movements. However, their coupling and combined contribution to memory formation remain largely unknown. Across four experiments combining eye tracking with scalp or intracranial electroencephalography during free or constrained viewing, we identify the degree of visual exploration, rather than subsequent memory performance, as consistent modulator of posterior alpha/beta power. Going beyond correlations, manipulating eye movements dissociated alpha/beta power reductions from memory. Together with the finding that saccade parameters predicted alpha/beta dynamics, our results directly link posterior alpha/beta activity to the oculomotor system. Moreover, the accumulation of saccades over time accounted for reduced alpha/beta power, resembling the canonical post-stimulus alpha/beta pattern. Our work demonstrates that posterior alpha/beta activity strongly reflects eye movements, supporting alternative perspectives on alpha/beta subsequent memory effects and the general function of posterior alpha/beta activity.

title: Direction of oscillatory networks in the human medial temporal lobe reverses across verbal working memory phases
The role of prefrontal sharp wave ripple-like events in working memory and behavioral performance.
abstract: Sharp wave ripples (SWRs) in the hippocampus are well known for their roles in memory processes; however, the occurrence and functional relevance of ripple-band events in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) during awake states remain unclear. Here we investigated the presence and characteristics of ripples in the PFC of monkeys performing a delayed-match-to-sample task. We analyzed local field potential signals, focusing on ripple activity, and compared ripple properties between a passive pre-training condition and the active post-training task, and, within post-training, between sessions with low and high behavioral performance. Ripple-triggered spiking increased in the post-training condition, peaking before the ripple, during the first stimulus (encoding), the working-memory delay (maintenance), and the second stimulus (retrieval). In the post-training condition, when the animals had to actively hold information in working memory, ripple peak frequency was consistently higher than in the passive pre-training condition during both the maintenance and the second-stimulus periods. Within the post-training task, higher behavioral performance was accompanied by lower ripple power during the maintenance period. Consistent with a physiological role for these events, ripple-band amplitude was phase-coupled to the ongoing delta rhythm. Together, these findings indicate that awake PFC SWR-like events are modulated by working-memory demand and task performance, and provide new insight into cortical ripple dynamics during active cognitive processing.

title: Theoretical frameworks for credit assignment via behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity
abstract: Abstract Behavioral Timescale Synaptic Plasticity (BTSP) is a form of plasticity which drives place field formation in hippocampal pyramidal neurons. Unlike traditional learning rules, BTSP learns pre-post correlations on timescales of seconds and rapidly changes single-unit activity in only a few trials. To study how BTSP-like learning can be integrated into network models, we propose a generalized theoretical framework, gBTSP, which we apply to unsupervised and supervised tasks in feedforward and recurrent networks. We show that unsupervised gBTSP learns place field maps in the feedforward case and attractor memories in the recurrent case. For supervised learning, we derive how plateau events can reduce task error, enabling gBTSP to solve trajectory matching and delayed non-match-to-sample tasks. Finally, we find that the speed of credit assignment via gBTSP is limited by network depth or CA3-like recurrence, suggesting that additional mechanisms are necessary to account for BTSP-driven few-shot learning in naturalistic settings.

title: A theory of generalized vector coding and subicular function.
abstract: Neural information processing is inextricably linked to the selectivity of individual neurons, as described by their receptive fields. Far from the sensory periphery, neural representations are the result of substantial upstream processing, mixed with internally generated information. Low-dimensional spatial codes in the hippocampal formation offer a handle on understanding these representations. The subiculum, a key but comparatively understudied hippocampal area, exhibits numerous, seemingly unrelated neural codes. Neurons like boundary vector cells, corner cells, or axis-tuned cells are named after the environmental features that appear to drive them, but a common account for their neuronal selectivity is lacking. Here, we propose Disco, a theory explaining subicular functions and related neural codes in other areas. Given the continuous flow of experience, subicular activity can be understood as signaling discontinuities in that flow, coded in a vector base. Geometric discontinuities drive responses to walls, drops, objects, holes, corners, and curved surfaces. The generality of Disco enables predictions for 3D environments, natural scenes, and mixed-modality coding. Discontinuities are not identical to the concept of boundaries (abstract or spatial), as illustrated by non-spatial discontinuities in behavioral state. These yield axis coding in the model (activity along parallel maze arms). Finally, tracking population activity signals event boundaries as discontinuities in neural space. The emergence of diverse neural activity suggests that discontinuity coding may serve as a key principle in the subiculum and related brain areas supporting (spatial) memory and navigation.
